lesson.title: Endergonic Reactions: Building Order Costs Energy
lesson.summary: An endergonic reaction absorbs free energy from its surroundings because its products end up holding more chemical potential energy than its reactants, so the reaction will not proceed without an outside energy source.
lesson.body:
An endergonic reaction is one with a positive change in Gibbs free energy, written as a positive delta G. That single sign carries a lot of meaning. It says that the products of the reaction contain more usable free energy than the reactants did, which means the reaction cannot run on its own. Left alone, reactants in an endergonic reaction simply sit there, because nature does not spontaneously push a system toward a higher energy, less probable state. Energy has to be added from somewhere else for the reaction to move forward at all.

This connects directly back to the Gibbs free energy relationship, delta G equals delta H minus T times delta S. When delta G comes out positive, either the reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings, or the products are more ordered than the reactants (a drop in entropy), or some combination of both. Endergonic reactions typically build complexity: they take small, simple, relatively low energy molecules and stitch them into larger, higher energy, more ordered structures. That is why endergonic chemistry is the chemistry of construction, while exergonic chemistry, covered next, tends to be the chemistry of breakdown.

A clear biological example is the light-independent phase of photosynthesis, where carbon dioxide and water are converted into glucose and oxygen. Overall, the synthesis of one mole of glucose from carbon dioxide and water requires an input of a very large amount of free energy, on the order of hundreds of kilocalories per mole. That energy has to come from somewhere, and in photosynthesis it comes from sunlight captured earlier in the light reactions. A simpler, everyday cellular example is dehydration synthesis, such as forming a peptide bond between two amino acids: the product has higher free energy than the separated amino acids, so joining them is endergonic and requires energy input rather than releasing it.

Cells cannot simply wait around for a rare burst of ambient energy to drive every endergonic step they need. Instead, they systematically pair endergonic reactions with strongly exergonic ones so that the combined, or coupled, process has a net negative delta G overall. The single most common energy source used for this pairing is the hydrolysis of ATP, a molecule built for exactly this purpose. The chapters that follow build up that machinery piece by piece: the structure of ATP, why breaking it apart releases usable energy, and how that released energy gets funneled into otherwise unfavorable reactions.

Zooming out, this is really a statement about how living things work against the general tendency of the universe to spread energy out and increase disorder. Anabolic pathways, the reactions that build macromolecules such as proteins, nucleic acids, and complex carbohydrates, are almost always endergonic overall, because assembling ordered polymers from simple monomers decreases entropy locally. Life sustains that local decrease in entropy only by constantly importing energy, whether from sunlight or from the chemical bonds of food, and by releasing heat and lower energy waste products back into the environment, which increases entropy elsewhere. Endergonic reactions are therefore not an exception to thermodynamics, they are exactly what you would expect from a system that pays for order with a continuous energy budget.
